title: First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum opens in New Delhi
where: 'PM Modi to open SCO Civilisational Dialogue today' (Divya A, 20 Nov, p. 8); 'Shekhawat: Youth, artists, digital push can preserve shared heritage' (Divya A, 22 Nov, p. 6)
syllabus: GS2 › Regional groupings involving India (SCO); India and its neighbourhood · GS1 › Indian culture: art forms, literature and architecture · GS4 › Ethics in international relations; soft power
summary: PM Modi inaugurated the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum at Purana Qila, with about 20 countries including Pakistan, whose minister attended an official event in Delhi for the first time since Operation Sindoor.
evolution: Modi proposes a dedicated platform for civilisational dialogue at the SCO Summit, Tianjin.
Proposal welcomed in the SCO's Bishkek Declaration.
Modi inaugurates the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum at Purana Qila; exhibition 'Astitva' on Delhi's history.
Thematic sessions; 13 ministers speak; Iran proposes three heritage initiatives.
ideas: India's initiative inside the SCO: born of Modi's Tianjin (2025) proposal and welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration, it adds a cultural pillar to a security-heavy grouping.
GS2 · SCO / Groupings
The Civilisational Dialogue Forum gives the SCO a people-to-people pillar beyond security and counter-terrorism.
Heritage as diplomacy: sessions on music, textiles, cuisine, scripts, manuscripts and monastic trails; 'Astitva' traces Delhi's history from 1200 BCE to 1200 CE.
GS1 · Culture / GS2 · Soft power
Shared heritage, from scripts to monastic trails, is soft power that builds trust where politics divides.
Multilateral room for adversaries: Pakistan's minister attended, and Delhi framed it as 'not a bilateral setting', asking all to extend due courtesy.
GS2 · India–Pakistan
Multilateral platforms let India engage Pakistan without changing its bilateral position.
Heritage is also contested: Pakistan has been asserting its Indus claim through Mohenjo-daro and Harappa; its minister invoked Taxila, Gandhara and Ghalib.
GS1 · Indus Valley / GS2 · Neighbourhood
Shared heritage can unite or be claimed; civilisational diplomacy must turn common roots into common ground.
Preserving heritage together: Shekhawat stressed youth, artisans, cultural tourism, digital initiatives and joint research; Iran proposed networks for manuscripts, translation and youth dialogue.
GS1 · Heritage conservation / GS2 · Central Asia
Digitising manuscripts and joint research make heritage a living bridge with Central Asia and West Asia.
keywords: Civilisational diplomacy
Using shared history and culture to build ties between states
GS2 · Soft power
Through the SCO forum, India practises civilisational diplomacy, turning shared heritage into strategic goodwill.
Track 1.5 cultural engagement
Ministers, scholars and artists together in one dialogue
GS2 · Diplomacy
Bringing ministers and scholars together, the forum blends official and cultural tracks of diplomacy.

The Indus Valley is contested heritage; dialogue can turn it from a claim into a shared legacy.
Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
'The world is one family', the forum's cultural theme
GS4 · Values in IR
The forum's theme, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, frames India's foreign policy as dialogue, not domination.

India's cultural pillar for the SCO

trend.t: SCO questions moved from basics (aims and importance for India, 2021) to its internal frictions (2023's 'virus of conflict'), while Central Asia appeared on its own (2018, 2024). Soft power has been asked as a tool for India–Pakistan goodwill (2015) and as an ethical component of national power (GS4, 2020).
trend.watch: The SCO has come up twice in three years (2021, 2023), and both times the question asked what India can do inside a divided grouping, so India's initiatives within the SCO are a must-study.
focus: India's role and initiatives within the SCO
Cultural and civilisational links with Central Asia
Soft power and people-to-people ties in neighbourhood policy
Engaging Pakistan on multilateral platforms

How can shared cultural heritage strengthen India's relations with Central Asia? (10 marks)
Examine the role of soft power in India's engagement with regional groupings. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Civilisational dialogue can serve as a bridge where political dialogue fails." Discuss in the context of India's initiative within the SCO.

answer.t: Proposed by India at the SCO's Tianjin Summit (2025) and welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration, the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum opened in New Delhi in November 2026 with about 20 countries, including Pakistan.

pts.t: Shared art, scripts and faith traditions remind states of what unites them beyond current disputes.
pts.ex: Sessions on monastic trails, manuscripts and shared architecture.

pts.t: A multilateral, cultural setting allows engagement without political concessions.
pts.ex: Pakistan's minister attended; Delhi called it 'not a bilateral setting'.

pts.t: Artists, scholars and youth build ties that outlast governments.
pts.ex: Iran's proposed Network for Dialogue Among Youths.

pts.t: A cultural pillar softens a grouping known for counter-terrorism and rivalry.
pts.ex: India's initiative adds culture to the SCO's agenda.

pts.t: History provides a natural bridge to Central Asia where connectivity is limited.
pts.ex: Purana Qila: Humayun from Central Asia, Sher Shah from Afghanistan.

pts.t: Positions India as a civilisational state offering dialogue.
pts.ex: Cultural theme 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'.

pts.t: A shared past can become a rival claim.
pts.ex: Pakistan asserting its Indus claim through Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.

pts.t: Terrorism and border disputes limit how far goodwill travels.
pts.ex: First Pakistani minister in Delhi since Operation Sindoor; Dargah visit not cleared.

pts.t: China–India and Russia–West tensions shape the SCO's agenda.
pts.ex: GS2-2023: 'virus of conflict' in the SCO.

pts.t: Forums risk becoming photo-ops without follow-up.
pts.ex: Need for institutional networks, not one-off events.

pts.t: States send non-culture ministers, signalling politics over culture.
pts.ex: Pakistan sent its Climate Change minister, not its culture minister.

pts.t: Weak transport and visa links limit exchanges with Central Asia.
pts.ex: Land access to Central Asia blocked through Pakistan.

pts.t: Annual meetings with a secretariat-backed work plan.
pts.ex: Build on the Bishkek Declaration.

pts.t: Digitise and translate shared manuscripts.
pts.ex: Iran's manuscript and translation proposals.

pts.t: Exchanges, scholarships and cultural tourism.
pts.ex: Shekhawat's focus on youth, artisans and digital initiatives.

pts.t: Keep cultural tracks open even when political ties are frozen.
pts.ex: Due courtesy to all delegations at the forum.

pts.t: Pair cultural ties with Chabahar and INSTC links to Central Asia.
pts.ex: India–Central Asia engagement.

pts.t: Joint archaeology and museum exchanges on common sites.
pts.ex: Gandhara and Taxila as shared heritage.

answer.t: As Pakistan's minister said at the forum, 'When history discovers us, it should find that we were talking'; civilisational dialogue keeps that conversation alive while politics catches up.

title: Shenzhen Peace Declaration: Trump, Xi, Putin agree on boosting oil supplies, reducing nuclear risks
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (AP); editorial 'G3 claims common ground, strikes no bargain' (p. 10); op-eds by Sujan Chinoy and Surupa Gupta (p. 11)
syllabus: GS2 › Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; important international institutions (UN, ICC) · GS3 › Energy security · GS4 › Ethics in international relations
summary: Meeting in Shenzhen on the APEC sidelines, Trump, Xi and Putin agreed to push UN reform, raise refined petroleum supplies, curb the ICC's reach and hold dialogue on nuclear risks.
evolution: Quad leaders meet in Manila; Trump returns to the Quad table before Shenzhen.
Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting.
ideas: Four-point agenda: UN reform, more refined petroleum, curbs on the ICC and 'similar bodies', and dialogue on nuclear risks and proliferation.
GS2 · Great powers / International institutions
The Shenzhen statement shows great powers setting a global agenda outside multilateral institutions.
Common ground, no grand bargain: compared with Yalta (1945), but the Express editorial and Sujan Chinoy see optics over substance, with no breakthrough on Ukraine.
GS2 · World order
Shenzhen is no Yalta: three rivals sought common ground, not a carve-up of the world.
Weakening of rules-based multilateralism: all three leaders prefer personalised, transactional deals over institutions such as the WTO, NATO or the ICC.
GS2 · Multilateralism
Personalised summitry by great powers erodes rules-based multilateralism that protects middle powers.
Accountability bypassed: none of the three is a party to the Rome Statute, and the ICC has a warrant against Putin.
GS2 · International institutions / GS4 · Ethics in IR
Curbing the ICC shields the powerful from accountability, a core ethical concern in international relations.
India's stake: as one of the world's largest refining hubs it gains from steadier fuel supply, but must guard against great-power hegemony through like-minded partnerships and 'strength within'.
GS2 · India's interests / GS3 · Energy security
India's answer to great-power deals is multi-alignment abroad and industrial strength at home.

GS2 · World order

trend.t: Questions on the world order moved from India's image in a changing order (2019) to great-power rivalry blocking UN reform (2025), the retreat from multilateralism to bilateralism in trade (GS3, 2025) and alternatives such as BRICS (2026). GS4 has paired this with ethics in IR: war (2022), power and moral duty (2020) and strategic interest over ethics (2026).
trend.watch: Great-power rivalry and the decline of multilateralism appeared in both GS2 and GS3 in 2025 and again in 2026, so the shift from rules to power-based deals is a must-study theme across papers.
focus: Decline of multilateralism and great-power deals
UN reform and the role of the P5

potential: "Great-power summitry outside multilateral institutions threatens the rules-based order." Discuss with reference to the recent US–China–Russia trilateral and its implications for India. (15 marks)

practice.q: "Great-power summitry outside multilateral institutions threatens the rules-based order." Discuss with reference to the recent US–China–Russia trilateral and its implications for India.
parts: How such summitry threatens the rules-based order
The other side: why it may not

answer.t: On 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi and Putin agreed on UN reform, more refined petroleum, curbs on the ICC and dialogue on nuclear risks, prompting comparisons with Yalta (1945).

answer.h: How such summitry threatens the rules-based order

pts.t: Decisions taken by three leaders sideline the UN, WTO and other forums where all states have a voice.
pts.ex: Agenda set at a trilateral, not in the UN General Assembly.

pts.t: Limiting international courts shields powerful states and leaders.
pts.ex: Joint call that the ICC 'must not abuse' its jurisdiction; ICC warrant against Putin.

pts.t: Great-power deals revive the idea that big states decide for small ones.
pts.ex: Russia's argument for negotiated spheres of influence.

pts.t: Leader-to-leader bargains replace stable, rule-based processes.
pts.ex: Surupa Gupta: all three epitomise personalised, transactional leadership.

pts.t: Dialogue replaces binding limits.
pts.ex: New START expired in February; no commitment to cut arsenals.

pts.t: Reform defined by the P5 may freeze out aspirants.
pts.ex: GS2-2025: UN reform stalled by East–West entanglement.

answer.h: The other side: why it may not

pts.t: The three met to find common ground, not to divide the world.
pts.ex: Editorial: 'claims common ground, strikes no bargain'.

pts.t: None can deliver its core aims, limiting real impact.
pts.ex: Sujan Chinoy: 'Shenzhen is no Yalta'.

pts.t: Indo-Pacific states increasingly write their own rules.
pts.ex: ASEAN centrality and multi-alignment on display in Manila.

pts.t: Even talk on nuclear risks lowers the chance of miscalculation.
pts.ex: Commitment to 'strategic stability and international security'.

pts.t: Steadier refined fuel supply helps India as a major refining hub.
pts.ex: Plan to raise refined petroleum output and supply.

pts.t: P5-led reform may sideline India's claim to a permanent seat.
pts.ex: Vague call for 'UN reform' by three P5 members.

pts.t: A US–China thaw can reduce India's weight in US strategy.
pts.ex: Trump–Xi one-on-one in Shenzhen, their third substantial meeting this year.

pts.t: A US–Russia opening may ease pressure on India's Russia links.
pts.ex: Trump–Putin sit-down in Shenzhen.

pts.t: Engage all poles through the Quad, ASEAN, BRICS and the SCO.
pts.ex: India's engagement across Manila forums.

pts.t: Build industrial and technological capacity so others cannot dictate terms.
pts.ex: Editorial: India's ability depends on 'the strength within'.

pts.t: Push inclusive reform of the UN and global finance.
pts.ex: India's voice for the Global South.

pts.t: Partner middle powers to defend rules on trade and the seas.
pts.ex: ASEAN, Japan, Australia.

pts.t: Spread sources and build reserves against supply shocks.
pts.ex: Strategic petroleum reserves.

pts.t: Back institutions that protect smaller states.
pts.ex: Support for UNCLOS and freedom of navigation.

answer.t: Shenzhen shows power seeking to set rules for all; India's answer lies in multi-alignment abroad and strength at home.

title: Quad unveils security, business, AI plans; Trump offers open line
where: Front page lead, continued on page 2 (Shubhajit Roy)
syllabus: GS2 › Bilateral, regional and global groupings involving India and/or affecting India's interests · GS3 › Security challenges in maritime areas; cyber security; science and technology (AI) · GS4 › Ethics in international relations
summary: At their first leaders' meeting since 2024, on the EAS sidelines in Manila, the Quad announced a maritime surveillance collaboration, an AI accelerator, enhanced cyber cooperation, critical mineral deals and a Business Leaders' Forum in Mumbai in 2027.

trend.t: Indo-Pacific questions began with the South China Sea and freedom of navigation (2014, 2016), moved to the Quad's own character (2020) and rival groupings such as AUKUS (2021), and in 2026 reached a specific Quad initiative, IPMDA, tested against India's SAGAR vision.
trend.watch: The Quad has been asked directly in 2020 and 2026, and the 2026 question picked one initiative and asked for a critical assessment, so the new surveillance collaboration, AI accelerator or critical minerals deals are the next likely angles.
focus: Quad's shift from security to technology, supply chains and economy
Maritime domain awareness: IPMDA and the 2027 surveillance exercise

potential: "The Quad is evolving from a maritime security dialogue into a partnership for technology, supply chains and economic security." Discuss. (15 marks)
Examine the significance of the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration for India's maritime security. (10 marks)
"Critical minerals have become the new frontier of strategic partnerships." Discuss with reference to the Quad. (10 marks)

practice.q: "The Quad is evolving from a maritime security dialogue into a partnership for technology, supply chains and economic security." Discuss.

answer.t: Started in 2007 and revived in 2017, the Quad met at leaders' level in Manila in November 2026 and announced plans spanning maritime surveillance, AI, cyber security, critical minerals and business.

pts.t: Shared surveillance gives the Indo-Pacific a common picture of what moves at sea, from dark shipping to illegal fishing.
pts.ex: Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration; P-8 and P-3C aircraft in a first Quad exercise in 2027.

pts.t: Regular drills let four navies operate together in anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare.
pts.ex: The 30th Malabar exercise near Japan.

pts.t: The Quad defends open sea lanes and overflight under international law.
pts.ex: Joint statement: 'open, safe and resilient maritime transit corridors'.

pts.t: It rejects unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion.
pts.ex: Joint statement on destabilising actions that escalate tensions.

pts.t: The grouping condemns terrorism in all forms, including cross-border terrorism.
pts.ex: A key gain for India given terror from across its western border.

pts.t: Disaster response gives the Quad a non-military face in the region.
pts.ex: Modi lists disaster response among the Quad's core areas.

pts.t: The Quad funds trusted AI access and deployment so the region does not depend on untrusted systems.
pts.ex: Quad AI accelerator to coordinate and fund trusted AI across the Indo-Pacific.

pts.t: Rising cyber incidents need shared standards and response.
pts.ex: Enhanced Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation for 'an open and secure cyberspace'.

pts.t: New deals diversify supply so no member is vulnerable to a single supplier.
pts.ex: Statement's concern over economic coercion through arbitrary export restrictions.

pts.t: Business ties turn diplomatic intent into investment and jobs.
pts.ex: Inaugural Quad Business Leaders' Forum in Mumbai, 2027.

pts.t: Deliverables for smaller states build legitimacy beyond the four members.
pts.ex: Modi: 'trusted solutions for the entire Indo-Pacific'.

pts.t: Supply chains are now treated as a security question.
pts.ex: MEA: cooperation in maritime security, economic security and critical technologies.

pts.t: The Quad is a loose partnership; commitments depend on political will.
pts.ex: Leaders met in Manila for the first time since 2024.

pts.t: Members differ in how far they want to confront China, given deep trade ties.
pts.ex: The Quad meets just before Trump's trilateral with Xi and Putin.

pts.t: India avoids any alliance commitment and keeps ties with Russia.
pts.ex: India's stand of independent foreign policy and multi-alignment.

pts.t: Shifts in US trade and alliance policy can strain partners.
pts.ex: US tariffs on Indian goods in 2025 tested India–US ties.

pts.t: South-East Asian states fear great-power rivalry eclipsing ASEAN centrality.
pts.ex: Modi's own stress on ASEAN unity and centrality at the EAS.

pts.t: Announcements can outrun implementation and funding.
pts.ex: Critics' 'Asian NATO' framing feeds Chinese pushback if delivery lags.

pts.t: Annual leaders' meetings and a light coordination mechanism keep momentum.
pts.ex: A two-year gap before Manila shows the cost of irregular meetings.

pts.t: Prioritise HADR, health, connectivity and training for smaller states.
pts.ex: Quad Vaccine Partnership as an earlier model.

pts.t: Anchor Quad plans in ASEAN-led platforms such as the EAS.
pts.ex: India's Act East Policy and IPOI.

pts.t: Shape norms for trusted, safe and human-centric technology.
pts.ex: India's AI Impact Summit stress on safe, inclusive AI.

pts.t: Joint processing and stockpiling of critical minerals, not just purchase deals.
pts.ex: Quad critical mineral deals announced in Manila.

pts.t: Present the Quad as a provider of public goods, not a military bloc.
pts.ex: Joint statement: 'a force for good and a partnership of action'.

answer.t: From Malabar drills to an AI accelerator and a Mumbai business forum, the Quad is widening its agenda, and its credibility now rests on delivery to the Indo-Pacific.

title: Look beyond old climate fault lines / Three steps COP should take for tangible outcomes
where: Editorial page, page 10 (editorial) and Ideas page, page 11 (Sumit Prasad, CEEW)
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental degradation (climate change, UNFCCC) · GS2 › Important international institutions and fora; India and the Global South · GS4 › Environmental ethics; climate justice
summary: Ahead of COP31 in Antalya, India has not committed to the '35 by 35' global electrification target, citing sovereignty and poverty eradication; the CEEW asks the 'COP of implementation' to show reports, finance and a scorecard.
evolution: First Loss and Damage payout goes to Nepal: climate justice needs quicker compensation.
Energy security depends on whether and how India electrifies (electrification thread).
ideas: National circumstances first: India is yet to back the '35 by 35' target (raise electricity's share of global energy use from 23% in 2023 to 35% by 2035), saying every country must weigh sovereignty and poverty eradication; developing countries face weaker grids and stressed utilities.
GS3 · Climate change / GS2 · India's stand in climate fora
India resists one-size targets like '35 by 35' because weak grids and poverty make national circumstances decisive.

An unfair critique: India is among a small group making steady progress on Paris commitments; calling its early delivery a sign of low ambition ignores bottlenecks in developed countries and the Global North's failure on finance and technology.
GS3 · Paris Agreement / climate justice
India's early delivery on Paris targets shows good faith, while the North's finance shortfall remains the real ambition gap.

Climate action is in India's own interest: greater urgency serves its development and strategy, and lets it lead the Global South through the International Solar Alliance and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure.
GS2 · India-led institutions / Global South
Through the ISA and CDRI, India can turn climate action into leadership of the Global South.

'Implementation COP' risks becoming a slogan: claimed at COP27, COP30 and COP31; 2035 NDCs were due in February 2025 and second transparency reports by December 31, yet by late October only Colombia and Turkey had filed.
GS2 · UNFCCC process
A COP can claim to be about implementation only if parties report on time; by late October only two had filed transparency reports.

Three steps for credibility: every party files its transparency report on time; developed countries report finance delivered and promised; the presidency publishes an annual scorecard for its voluntary 2035 targets and Climate Implementation Bridge.
GS2 · Global governance / GS3 · Climate finance
Scorecards for voluntary pledges and reports on delivered finance would turn COP summits from promises into accountability.
keywords: Biennial Transparency Report (BTR)
Report under the Paris Agreement on emissions and progress against NDCs
GS3 · Climate governance
Timely Biennial Transparency Reports are the evidence an 'implementation COP' needs.
Action Agenda
The voluntary, non-negotiated track where presidencies rally pledges from states and non-state actors
GS2 · Climate diplomacy
The Action Agenda gains traction fast but delivers little without a scorecard.
National circumstances
Paris principle that each country's targets reflect its capacities and development needs
GS3 · Climate justice

Climate finance credibility
Whether developed countries deliver the money they promise
GS3 · Climate finance / GS2
For developing countries, climate finance delivered, not pledged, is the barometer of global good faith.

trend.t: Climate questions moved from mechanisms (carbon credits and CDM, 2014) and impacts on India (2017) to COP outcomes and India's commitments (COP26 and the Green Grid, 2021), India's stance in international fora (2022) and a review of Paris commitments and NDCs (2025).
trend.watch: COPs and the Paris Agreement were asked in 2021, 2022 and 2025, so they are a must-study area. Questions ask what a COP decided, what India committed and how India positions itself, so track NDCs, finance and India-led initiatives.
focus: India's NDCs and progress (non-fossil capacity, emissions intensity, net zero 2070)

India-led initiatives: ISA, CDRI, Green Grid
Global South and climate justice (CBDR-RC)

How can India use the International Solar Alliance and CDRI to lead the Global South on climate action? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Climate summits have shifted from negotiation to implementation, but delivery lags." Discuss the challenges in making COPs deliver and the role India can play.

answer.t: Turkey has branded COP31 in Antalya the 'COP of Implementation', a label also claimed at COP27 and COP30, yet only about 5% of 203 cooperative climate initiatives since 2015 have met their goals (CEEW).

pts.t: Developed countries have repeatedly missed finance and technology commitments, eroding trust.

pts.t: Action Agenda pledges are consensus-free and unenforced.
pts.ex: COP31's voluntary 2035 targets.

pts.t: UNFCCC forums share progress but none enforces delivery.
pts.ex: Facilitative, Multilateral Consideration of Progress.

pts.t: The North presses the South on NDCs while the South sees scrutiny shifted from the North's own record.
India is among few countries making steady progress on Paris commitments.
pts.ex: 50% non-fossil installed capacity reached in 2025, five years early.

pts.t: India defends each country's right to set its energy mix and development path.
pts.ex: Undecided on the '35 by 35' target.

pts.t: India can press for finance delivered, not promised.
pts.ex: Voice of Global South Summits.

pts.t: India-led bodies can turn plans into projects.

pts.t: Timely reporting strengthens India's moral authority to demand the same of others.

pts.t: Anchor COP discussions in synthesis reports of NDCs and BTRs.
Developed countries to file biennial communications on finance delivered and promised.
Annual progress reports on voluntary targets.
pts.ex: Proposed for COP31's 2035 targets.

pts.t: Convert national priorities into investable projects.
pts.ex: COP31's Climate Implementation Bridge.

pts.t: Affordable access to storage, grids and clean technologies.
Equal weight to adaptation for vulnerable states.
pts.ex: Small island states and LDCs.

answer.t: A COP's success must be measured by what the crisis demands; India can make 'implementation' mean delivered emissions cuts and delivered finance.

title: An alliance for multilateralism by other means
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora: their structure and mandate; Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
summary: The Partners for Multilateralism (P4M), launched at the 81st UNGA week and co-sponsored by India among others, commits to strengthening multilateral cooperation; the author argues it needs a concrete plan, clear principles and public engagement to succeed.
evolution: BRICS Parliamentary Forum seeks UNSC reform.
P4M, co-sponsored by India, pledges to strengthen multilateral cooperation.
ideas: Multilateralism under severe pressure: the US, a principal founder and long-time guarantor of the system, is rejecting it in word and deed, and other major players flout rules with impunity.
GS2 · International institutions
With the system's own guarantor walking away, middle and smaller powers must carry multilateralism.
A bridge across divides: co-sponsored by Australia, Brazil, Barbados, Canada, the EU, India and Kenya and signed by 18 more, P4M joins large and small countries of the Global South and North.
GS2 · Groupings involving India
P4M's mixed membership makes it a rare bridge between the Global North and South.

Reform language reflects a power shift: its pledge of cooperation that is 'open, fair, equitable, inclusive' echoes the South's long demand, now heard in a North weakened by Western turmoil and Transatlantic strain.
GS2 · Global order / Global South
The North's new receptiveness to reform reflects the Global South's growing clout and the West's own turmoil.
Plan and principles, or failure: P4M needs an action plan with costs and how they are shared, and clear principles that set it apart from efforts such as China's four Global Initiatives.
GS2 · Effect of policies of other countries
Coalitions without costed plans and clear principles join the list of well-intended but failed initiatives.
Engage people and the planet: reform drives fail when they ignore affected populations; P4M's diversity could offer ideas on deep ecology and interspecies coexistence for a new framework.
GS2 · Global governance / GS4 · Environmental ethics
Multilateralism will regain legitimacy only when it engages the public and protects the planet, not just states.
keywords: Minilateralism / coalition of the willing
Small, flexible groups of like-minded states acting where universal bodies stall
GS2 · Groupings
When universal institutions stall, coalitions of the willing like P4M keep cooperation alive.
Rules-based order
An international system governed by agreed norms rather than power
GS2 · International order
P4M's commitment to institutions and rule of law defends the rules-based order.
Reformed multilateralism
India's call to update global institutions to reflect today's realities
GS2 · India's foreign policy
India's co-sponsorship of P4M fits its long call for reformed multilateralism.
Bridging power
A country able to connect rival blocs
GS2 · India's global role
India's presence in P4M, BRICS and the Quad shows its role as a bridging power.
Deep ecology
A view that nature has value in itself, not only for human use
GS4 · Environmental ethics
Deep ecology asks global institutions to protect the planet for its own sake.
examples: Partners for Multilateralism (P4M)
Launched at the 81st UNGA week, co-sponsored by India
GS2 · International institutions · groupings · Essay
P4M shows middle powers trying to save multilateralism as the great powers turn away from it.
US rejection of the system it built
A founder and guarantor turning away
GS2 · Global order · Essay
The US turning against institutions it founded shows that even the architects of an order can abandon it.
China's four Global Initiatives
Rival visions of global governance
GS2 · India–China · global order
China's Global Initiatives show the contest over who will write the next rules of global governance.
pyqs: Unresolved UN reform amid East–West imbalance and the US vs Russo-Chinese entanglement.
BRICS as a counterweight in global governance amplifying the Global South.
Challenges as the world moves from free trade and multilateralism to protectionism and bilateralism.
Key areas of WTO reform amid trade war, keeping India's interests in mind.
Has India's image as leader of the marginalised nations faded in the new global order?
Waning globalisation and the rise of sovereign nationalism.

trend.t: Questions moved from the mandates of specific bodies (WTO, Bretton Woods, UNESCO, 2013–2019) to the crisis of the system itself: WTO reform amid trade war (2018), unresolved UN reform and great-power rivalry (2025), the retreat from multilateralism (2025) and BRICS as a voice of the Global South (2026).
trend.watch: Since 2025 UPSC asks about the crisis of multilateralism almost every year. Prepare why the order is weakening, who is reshaping it and India's role as a bridge for the Global South.
focus: Crisis of multilateralism and great-power retreat
Reform of the UN, WTO and other institutions
New coalitions and groupings (BRICS, P4M)
India and the Global South

potential: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role. (15 marks)
What are the limits of coalitions of the willing in reforming global governance? (10 marks)
"In international relations, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." How can a rules-based order change this? (10 marks, GS4)

practice.q: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role.

answer.t: In September 2026, India, the EU, Brazil, Canada, Kenya, Australia and Barbados co-sponsored the Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) at the 81st UNGA, just as the US, the system's founder, turns away from it.

pts.t: The US rejects institutions it built, in word and deed.
pts.ex: Withdrawals from the WHO and the Paris Agreement.

pts.t: Rules are flouted with frequency and impunity.
pts.ex: Wars in Europe and West Asia.

pts.t: Key bodies cannot act or reform.
pts.ex: WTO Appellate Body non-functional since 2019; UNSC reform stalled.

pts.t: Institutions reflect 1945, not today's balance of power.
Competing models of global governance divide states.
pts.ex: China's four Global Initiatives.

pts.t: Institutions seem distant from the people they affect.
Mixed membership builds trust across old divides.
pts.ex: P4M joins large and small states of both.

pts.t: Commitment to cooperation that is open, fair, equitable and inclusive.
Small coalitions act faster than universal bodies.
Groupings amplify developing countries' demands.
pts.ex: BRICS; India's Voice of the Global South summits.

pts.t: Declarations without costed plans fade.
Without clarity, they overlap with rival initiatives.
Ignoring affected people breeds discontent.
Many small coalitions can weaken universal institutions.
India sits in the Quad, BRICS, SCO and P4M and can link rival blocs.
Push the South's agenda on finance, climate and technology.
pts.ex: African Union's G20 membership under India's 2023 presidency.

pts.t: Press for UNSC and WTO reform with like-minded partners.
pts.ex: G4 for UNSC reform.

pts.t: Back P4M with concrete projects, costs and burden-sharing.
Bring civilisational ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and LiFE into global norms.
pts.ex: G20 theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.

pts.t: Keep commitments, as on climate targets met early.
pts.ex: Paris capacity target met in 2025.

answer.t: As great powers retreat, coalitions like P4M can keep multilateralism alive; India, as a bridging power, can help turn declarations into a fairer, workable order.

title: Why Delhi mustn't take its eyes off Pakistan-Maldives
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Aditya Gowdara Shivamurthy, ORF)
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Bilateral, regional and global groupings · GS3 › Security challenges; Maritime security
summary: Maldives President Muizzu's state visit to Pakistan, with 20 MoUs including defence, shows the Maldives diversifying beyond India; the writer backs India's economic approach but says it must state its security red lines.
ideas: Diversification beyond India: Muizzu's visit produced 20 MoUs, from socio-economic sectors to cybersecurity, drugs and defence and maritime security, and a plan to scale up trade.
GS2 · India–Maldives
Small neighbours are hedging by diversifying partners, testing India's primacy in its neighbourhood.
A crowded defence space: the Maldives also has defence MoUs with China and Turkey, has bought armoured vehicles from the UAE and joined a Saudi-led maritime coalition.
GS2 · Neighbourhood / GS3 · Maritime security
Multiple defence partners for the Maldives crowd the Indian Ocean Region close to India's maritime boundaries.

Pakistan's wider play: since Operation Sindoor, Pakistan and China have held trilaterals with Bangladesh and Afghanistan; Pakistan has pushed SAARC revival, a South Asian bloc without India and a larger naval presence in the Bay of Bengal.
GS2 · Regional groupings
Pakistan is using new regional formats to dilute India's centrality in South Asia.

India's pragmatic economic diplomacy: T-bill extensions, debt restructuring, credit lines and currency swaps build leverage and goodwill without fuelling anti-India nationalism ahead of Maldivian elections.
GS2 · Neighbourhood First / Economic diplomacy
India's economic support builds leverage while avoiding the nationalist backlash that pressure would provoke.
Clear red lines on security: some MoUs (cybercrime, drugs) may even help India, but defence ties with Pakistan need clear communication of India's concerns.
GS2 · Foreign policy / GS3 · Security
India can accept the Maldives' diversification but must draw red lines on defence and security.
keywords: Strategic hedging
Small states balancing among several powers
GS2 · IR
The Maldives' outreach to Pakistan, China and Turkey is classic strategic hedging.
Neighbourhood First

GS2 · Foreign policy
Neighbourhood First relies on economic support to keep small neighbours close.

India's currency swaps and credit lines to the Maldives are economic statecraft.

India must communicate red lines on Pakistan's defence role in the Maldives.
Crowded IOR
More extra-regional powers active in the Indian Ocean
GS2 · Indian Ocean

Coercion would feed anti-India politics before elections.

Defence MoUs with Pakistan, China and Turkey bring rivals closer.
A bloc without India and a larger naval presence.

pts.t: On defence presence and bases.
Health, connectivity and climate resilience.
Coast-guard and maritime-domain-awareness links.

answer.t: India should stay the Maldives' most generous partner while making clear that its security in the Indian Ocean is not negotiable.
